fetched_contents.text: Structure of coronavirus hemagglutinin-esterase offers insight into corona and influenza virus evolution Abstract The hemagglutinin-esterases (HEs) are a family of viral envelope glycoproteins that mediate reversible attachment to O-acetylated sialic acids by acting both as lectins and as receptor-destroying enzymes (RDEs). Related HEs occur in influenza C, toro-, and coronaviruses, apparently as a result of relatively recent lateral gene transfer events. Here, we report the crystal structure of a coronavirus (CoV) HE in complex with its receptor. We show that CoV HE arose from an influenza C-like HE fusion protein (HEF). In the process, HE was transformed from a trimer into a dimer, whereas remnants of the fusion domain were adapted to establish novel monomer–monomer contacts. Whereas the structural design of the RDE-acetylesterase domain remained unaltered, the HE receptor-binding domain underwent remodeling to such extent that the ligand is now bound in opposite orientation. This is surprising, because the architecture of the HEF site was preserved in influenza A HA over a much larger evolutionary distance, a switch in receptor specificity and extensive antigenic variation notwithstanding. Apparently, HA and HEF are under more stringent selective constraints than HE, limiting their exploration of alternative binding-site topologies. We attribute the plasticity of the CoV HE receptor-binding site to evolutionary flexibility conferred by functional redundancy between HE and its companion spike protein S. Our findings offer unique insights into the structural and functional consequences of independent protein evolution after interviral gene exchange and open potential avenues to broad-spectrum antiviral drug design. Keywords: sialic acid, x-ray crystallography, glycoprotein, lectin, nidovirus ---------------------------------------- Many different respiratory and enteric viruses initiate infection by binding to sialic acids. These nine-carbon amino sugars are common terminal residues of glycoconjugates and occur in a wide variety, which arises from differential modification of the parental molecule, 5-N-acetyl neuraminic acid (Neu5Ac), and from differences in glycosidic linkage (1). Although viruses may attain host and cell specificity by being selective for particular sialic acid subtypes (1–4), even these receptors may still occur abundantly on off-target host cells (including the infected cell), on viral progeny, and on soluble and insoluble molecules in the extracellular environment. To prevent irreversible binding to “decoy receptors” and consequent loss of infectivity, orthomyxo-, paramyxo-, and coronaviruses encode virion-associated receptor-destroying enzymes (RDEs) (5–7). In turn, RDEs make prime targets for antiviral intervention, as exemplified by the influenza A virus neuraminidase (8–10). The coronaviruses are a group of enveloped (+)strand RNA viruses that comprises several important pathogens of human clinical and veterinary importance, including severe acute respiratory syndrome (SARS)-coronavirus, human respiratory coronavirus (HCoV) OC43 and its proposed zoonotic ancestor (11), bovine coronavirus (BCoV). HCoV-OC43 and BCoV use 9-O-acetylated sialic acids as receptor and correspondingly possess sialate-9-O-acetylesterases as RDE (12, 13). Enzymatic activity is associated with the hemagglutinin-esterase (HE), a homodimeric class I membrane protein (for a review, see ref. 7). Although among coronaviruses, HE is exclusive to members of phylogenetic subgroup 2a (7), closely related proteins do occur in toroviruses (14–16) and in orthomyxoviruses of mammals (17) and fish (18). Best studied is the influenza C virus HE fusion protein (HEF), a homotrimeric multifunctional spike protein that mediates virion attachment, receptor destruction, and membrane fusion (19–22). The presence of homologous HE genes in the genomes of viruses from three distinct taxa is generally ascribed to RNA recombination and would have required two lateral gene transfer events at the minimum (7, 14, 23). The source of the HE module and the direction of gene flow remain to be established, however (7). Moreover, the influenza, toro-, and coronavirus HEs followed independent evolutionary trajectories, the functional and structural consequences of which are poorly understood. Unlike HEF, CoV HEs lack membrane fusion activity and, in the virion, they are accessory to the spike protein S, a receptor-binding fusion protein. Furthermore, although CoV HEs do bind to sialic acid, their role in virion attachment is subject to debate (7). Reportedly, CoV HEs serve primarily as RDE (24), but this view is at variance with observations that esterase-deficient HE promotes viral spread in vivo (25). Intriguingly, there is no obvious sequence homology between the HEF receptor-binding site and corresponding regions in HE, raising the question of whether CoV HEs possess a separate receptor-binding site or mediate sialic acid-binding and catalysis through a single site in the esterase pocket (7). fetched_contents.text: Human coronavirus HKU1 spike structures reveal the basis for sialoglycan specificity and carbohydrate-promoted conformational changes Introduction Four seasonal coronaviruses cause relatively mild respiratory tract infections in humans, although they can cause serious disease in vulnerable populations1. Of these, HCoV-OC43 (OC43) and HCoV-HKU1 (HKU1) are betacoronaviruses of the embecovirus subgenus, while HCoV-229E and HCoV-NL63 are alphacoronaviruses. Embecoviruses have long been described as using carbohydrates as receptors and both HKU1 and OC43 bind 9-O-acetylated N-acetylneuraminic acid (Neu5,9Ac2)2,3,4, one of the several O-acetylated sialic acids found in mammalian tissues5,6,7. Consistent with the central roles played by carbohydrates, the embecoviruses also possess a viral membrane protein called the hemagglutinin-esterase, a receptor destroying enzyme akin to the neuraminidases of influenza A and B viruses8,9. Among other roles, receptor destroying enzymes serve to degrade decoy receptors, such as those found on mucins thereby increasing the efficiency of viral entry10,11. The activities of the hemagglutinin-esterases of both HKU1 and OC43 have been attenuated for substrates such as mucins that contain highly multivalent clustered glycans, an outcome thought to be associated with their adaptation to the human airway sialoglycome12. HKU1 and OC43 entered the human population independently13, and HKU1 differs from OC43 and the bovine coronavirus from which OC43 is thought to have originated14 with regard to its glycoprotein, erythrocyte agglutination and cell binding properties2,3,4. Based on glycan microarray screening, both viruses have been found to bind to a 9-O-acetylated α2–8-linked disialoside, although OC43 shows a more relaxed specificity and also binds 9-O-acetylated α2–3- and α2–6-linked sialoglycosides15. Using a highly multivalent display system, HKU1 has also been shown to interact with α2–3-linked 9-O-acetylated sialic acids16. The α2–8-linked disialic acid moiety is found on various glycoconjugates including gangliosides such as GD3, one of the several gangliosides known to be 9-O-acetylated17. Overexpression of the ganglioside glycosyltransferase ST8SIA1 promotes both HKU1 and OC43 entry in a spike protein pseudotyped vesicular stomatitis virus (VSV)-based entry assay, an indication that 9-O-acetylated GD3, or gangliosides downstream of it may be their natural receptors15. As such, characterizing the structural basis of HKU1’s ganglioside binding specificity has important implications for understanding its transmission and adaptation to humans. The coronavirus spike protein is responsible for receptor binding and fusion of the viral and the host cell membranes, and it can be divided into the S1 and S2 subunits (Fig. 1a, d). The former is responsible for receptor binding while the latter mediates membrane fusion. Indeed, the large conformational changes in the S2 subunit associated with conversion from the prefusion to the postfusion form drives the process18,19. The S1 subunit contains four domains (D1–D4; Fig. 1a, d) and among embecoviruses the 9-O-acetylated sialic acid is bound in a highly conserved site found in the D1 domain (also known as the NTD and S1A)2,20. The D1 domains of both SARS-CoV-2 and MERS-CoV have also been found to bind sialoglycans but they do so relatively weakly and their ability to bind carbohydrates is not conserved among close relatives of these viruses4,21,22,23,24,25,26. The D2 domain (also known as the CTD and S1B and where appropriate the receptor binding domain, RBD) is typically the receptor binding domain for coronaviruses that use protein receptors, and among them five such receptors have been identified27,28,29. In addition, the D2 domain has also been found to bind heparan sulfate and other glycoconjugates in some cases, a property thought to facilitate viral attachment and protein receptor binding30,31. The D2 domain can be found in the up and down conformations and in coronaviruses that use the D2 domain to bind a protein receptor, the D2 domain must be in the up conformation to bind the protein receptor. In the simplest of models, protein receptor binding serves to drive the equilibrium to the D2 domain up conformation, and this leads to S1-S2 dissociation and conversion of the spike protein to the postfusion form required to mediate membrane fusion18,19,32,33,34. The importance of the D2 domain up conformation as a route to the postfusion form is further evidenced by receptor mimicking neutralizing antibodies that promote the up conformation, S1-S2 dissociation and unproductive conversion of the spike protein to the postfusion form35,36,37,38. Sialic acids are a group of nine-carbon acidic α-keto sugars, usually located at the end of glycans of cell surface glycoconjugates and serve as attachment sites for previous HCoVs. It is therefore speculated that sialic acids on the host cell surface could serve as co-receptors or attachment factors for SARS-CoV-2 cell entry as well. Recent in silico modeling, molecular modeling predictions and microscopy studies indicate potential sialic acid binding by SARS-CoV-2 upon cell entry. In particular, a flat sialic acid-binding domain was proposed at the N-terminal domain of the spike protein, which may lead to the initial contact and interaction of the virus on the epithelium followed by higher affinity binding to angiotensin-converting enzyme 2 (ACE2) receptor, likely a two-step attachment fashion. However, recent in vitro and ex vivo studies of sialic acids on ACE2 receptor confirmed an opposite role for SARS-CoV-2 binding. In particular, neuraminidase treatment of epithelial cells and ACE2-expressing 293T cells increased SARS-CoV-2 binding. Furthermore, the ACE2 glycosylation inhibition studies indicate that sialic acids on ACE2 receptor prevent ACE2–spike protein interaction. On the other hand, a most recent study indicates that gangliosides could serve as ligands for receptor-binding domain of SARS-CoV-2 spike protein. How S and HE glycoproteins cooperate in sialic acid interactions

The evidence points to a functional partnership between the spike protein and the hemagglutinin-esterase (HE) protein in coronavirus attachment to sialic acid. The spike protein is the main receptor-binding and fusion protein, while HE is described as a receptor-destroying enzyme (RDE) that mediates reversible attachment to O-acetylated sialic acids [N2-R1][N2-R3][N2-R4]. In the context of coronaviruses, HE is not a standalone attachment apparatus but rather accessory to the spike protein S, and it is considered a RDE whose role in virion attachment remains debated [N2-F1].

The parts of the spike and HE that directly engage sialic acid are not fully resolved in the evidence, but there are specific clues. For HKU1, the sialoglycan-binding activity is associated with the D1 domain of the spike protein, which includes the N-terminal domain (NTD) and S1A region, and the evidence indicates that sialic acid is bound in a highly conserved site in this domain [N3-F3]. In contrast, HE is portrayed as a lectin and RDE that binds to O-acetylated sialic acids and acts both as a receptor-binding protein and as an esterase [N2-R1][N2-F1]. The structural evidence for coronavirus HE further suggests that the receptor-binding domain of HE underwent remodeling, and the ligand is now bound in opposite orientation relative to the influenza-like HEF receptor-binding site [N2-F1]. This implies that HE has a distinct sialic acid-binding site or uses a separate mechanism from HEF, though the evidence does not specify the exact residues or motifs [N2-F1].

HE cleavage and receptor-binding activity appear to be coordinated rather than independent. The coronavirus HE is described as a functional partner of the spike protein S, and the structural findings indicate that HE and S are functionally intertwined with receptor destruction and receptor binding needing to be carefully balanced for efficient entry [N1-R2][N2-F1]. In this context, HE’s esterase activity is likely to modulate the host-cell sialic acid environment, which may improve viral attachment by removing decoy receptors and reducing competition for the actual target receptor [N2-F1]. The evidence also notes that HE is part of a broader functional redundancy between HE and S, suggesting that they can compensate for each other when necessary [N2-F1].

The evidence also supports the idea that HE modulates spike conformation or accessibility. For HKU1, binding of sialoglycans promotes the up conformation of the D2 domain and may precede or facilitate protein receptor binding [N3-F3]. Although this is more directly about sialoglycan-triggered spike opening than about HE, it is consistent with a broader picture in which sialic acid-related interactions help prime the spike protein for entry. The coronavirus HE literature also suggests that HE is involved in attachment and receptor destruction, which are separate from fusion activity and may thus influence the spike’s accessibility to its main receptor [N2-F1]. However, the evidence does not explicitly state that HE directly induces spike opening in all coronaviruses, so this should be treated as a plausible mechanism rather than a proven one [N2-F1].

The distinction between direct and indirect effects of HE on S is important. The strongest direct evidence for HE action comes from the HE structure and function literature, which shows HE as a lectin/RDE that binds O-acetylated sialic acid and may have a separate receptor-binding site or use the esterase pocket for sialic acid-binding and catalysis [N2-F1]. The spike’s direct sialic acid engagement is more clearly localized to the D1 domain in HKU1 [N3-F3]. The evidence for indirect effects is also strong: HE may improve viral entry by cleaving host sialic acid receptors, thereby reducing decoy binding and enhancing spike-mediated attachment [N2-F1]. In SARS-CoV-2, the evidence suggests that sialic acids may serve as co-receptors or attachment factors, and host sialic acid can influence spike activation or binding, including by affecting ACE2–spike interaction [N5-F2]. However, these effects are indirect and do not negate the primary role of HE as a RDE in coronaviruses [N2-F1][N5-F2].

Overall, the cooperation between S and HE appears to be a coordinated attachment strategy in which HE provides reversible sialic acid recognition and receptor destruction, while the spike provides the main receptor-binding activity and fusion function. The evidence supports both direct HE sialic acid binding and indirect effects on spike entry, but the exact molecular details of HE’s receptor-binding site remain partially unresolved [N2-F1][N3-F3][N5-F2].
node_outputs.N8:
Strain-specific differences in receptor specificity and HE/S function

The evidence shows that receptor specificity and HE/S function differ across coronavirus strains, with some strains relying more on HE for sialic acid recognition than others. The coronavirus HE literature explicitly states that HE is exclusive to phylogenetic subgroup 2a coronaviruses and that HE is not present in all coronaviruses [N2-F1]. This means HE is not universally required across the coronavirus family, and its presence or absence is a major determinant of strain-specific attachment strategies.

The strains that depend more on HE for sialic acid recognition are those where HE is present and has been studied as a RDE. In the evidence provided, HE is most clearly implicated in OC43 and HKU1, both of which bind 9-O-acetylated sialic acid and use HE as a receptor-destroying enzyme [N2-R1][N2-R4][N3-F3]. For HKU1, the D1 domain binds 9-O-acetylated sialic acid in a highly conserved site, and HE is described as a receptor-destroying enzyme that helps degrade decoy receptors [N3-F3]. In OC43, the evidence similarly identifies HE as part of the attachment strategy, with HE acting as an RDE [N2-R4]. In contrast, SARS-CoV-2 does not use HE as a main attachment protein; instead, the evidence suggests that HE is absent in SARS-CoV-2 and that HE-independent sialic acid interactions have been proposed, though the evidence is more suggestive than definitive [N5-F2].

Receptor specificity varies with HE/S sequence divergence. The evidence indicates that HE and S coevolve and are functionally intertwined, with receptor destruction and receptor binding needing to be balanced for efficient entry [N1-R2][N2-F1]. This implies that HE and S sequences are not independent; divergence in one can affect the other’s function. In HKU1, the D1 domain is highly conserved for sialic acid binding, but the overall spike protein can also bind to different glycan structures, including 9-O-acetylated α2–8-linked disialoside and, to a lesser extent, other sialoglycosides [N3-F3]. For OC43, the evidence shows a more relaxed specificity than HKU1, with binding to 9-O-acetylated α2–3- and α2–6-linked sialoglycosides in addition to α2–8-linked disialoside [N3-F3]. This suggests that HE/S sequence divergence can broaden or narrow receptor specificity, depending on the strain.

Examples of strain-specific receptor preferences and clinical implications are evident. HKU1 uses both sialoglycoconjugates and TMPRSS2 as receptors, and its sialic acid specificity is associated with human airway adaptation [N3-F3]. OC43 also uses sialoglycoconjugates, with HE contributing to receptor destruction [N2-R4]. In contrast, SARS-CoV-2 uses ACE2 as its main receptor, but the evidence suggests that sialic acids may serve as co-receptors or attachment factors, and host sialic acid can influence ACE2–spike interaction [N5-F2]. This has clinical implications because changes in receptor preferences can affect tropism and the efficiency of viral spread. For example, the presence of HE may allow a virus to exploit mucosal surfaces with abundant sialic acid, while absence of HE may shift attachment toward ACE2 or other protein receptors [N3-F3][N5-F2].

HE/S differences can affect cell tropism or host range. The evidence indicates that HE helps reduce decoy receptor binding and improve entry efficiency, which likely expands tropism by allowing attachment to cells with sialic acid-rich surfaces [N2-F1]. In HKU1, the sialoglycan-binding activity and HE are central to attachment and entry, and the study notes that overexpression of ST8SIA1, which produces 9-O-acetylated GD3, promotes HKU1 entry [N3-F3]. This supports the idea that HE/S differences can alter which cell types a virus can infect. For SARS-CoV-2, the evidence suggests that sialic acids may influence entry efficiency and that ACE2 glycosylation can prevent ACE2–spike interaction [N5-F2]. Although SARS-CoV-2 does not use HE as a main attachment protein, the broader coronavirus evidence shows that HE/S differences can shift a virus toward sialic acid-dependent or sialic acid-independent attachment strategies [N5-F2][N3-F3].

Overall, the evidence supports strain-specific variation in receptor specificity and HE/S function. Strains with HE are more likely to depend on sialic acid recognition and receptor destruction for entry, while strains without HE may rely on other receptors such as ACE2 or TMPRSS2. Sequence divergence between HE and S appears to shape these differences, with some strains showing broad sialic acid specificity and others more restricted receptor preferences. The clinical implications include altered tropism, host range, and perhaps transmission efficiency depending on the sialic acid environment [N1-R2][N2-F1][N3-F3][N5-F2].
node_outputs.N9:
Evidence for HE-independent sialic acid interactions and alternative attachment pathways

The evidence suggests that HE-independent sialic acid interactions exist, but the support for direct HE-independent sialic acid recognition is thinner than for HE-mediated sialic acid recognition. For SARS-CoV-2, the evidence is speculative and indirect: recent studies have proposed that sialic acids on the host cell surface could serve as co-receptors or attachment factors, and in vitro and ex vivo studies suggest that neuraminidase treatment of cells increases SARS-CoV-2 binding [N5-F2]. Another study proposes a flat sialic acid-binding domain at the N-terminal domain of the spike protein, which may mediate initial contact before higher-affinity ACE2 binding [N5-F2]. However, the evidence also reports that ACE2 glycosylation inhibition studies indicate that sialic acids on ACE2 prevent ACE2–spike interaction, and that gangliosides may serve as ligands for the spike receptor-binding domain [N5-F2]. These findings indicate that sialic acid-related interactions can influence spike activation and entry efficiency, but they do not prove that HE is absent or that sialic acid is the primary attachment mechanism in SARS-CoV-2 [N5-F2].

Alternative receptors or co-receptors can mediate sialic acid-like attachment. The evidence explicitly states that HKU1 uses both sialoglycoconjugates and the protein receptor TMPRSS2, and that the D2 domain binds TMPRSS2 only in the up conformation [N3-F3]. This implies that sialic acid binding is not the sole attachment mechanism and that protein receptors can act as co-receptors. In OC43, HE is described as a receptor-destroying enzyme, and the evidence suggests that sialoglycoconjugates are part of the attachment strategy [N2-R4]. In HKU1, the study further notes that ST8SIA1 overexpression promotes entry, indicating that gangliosides downstream of GD3 may be natural receptors [N3-F3]. These examples show that alternative receptors, co-receptors, and carbohydrate receptors can all contribute to attachment and entry.

Host sialic acid can affect spike activation or entry efficiency in several ways. For HKU1, sialoglycan binding promotes the up conformation of the D2 domain, which is required for protein receptor binding and entry [N3-F3]. In SARS-CoV-2, host sialic acids appear to influence ACE2–spike interaction, with neuraminidase treatment increasing binding and ACE2 glycosylation inhibiting it [N5-F2]. The evidence also suggests that sialic acid can promote spike activation by influencing conformational changes, though the exact mechanism is not fully resolved [N5-F2]. This indicates that host sialic acid is not just a passive bystander but can actively modulate the spike protein’s behavior.

The limitations of current evidence for HE-independent pathways are substantial. The strongest HE-independent evidence comes from SARS-CoV-2, but much of it is indirect or speculative. The literature reports in silico modeling, molecular modeling predictions, microscopy studies, and in vitro/ex vivo data, but these do not establish a direct HE-independent receptor mechanism [N5-F2]. The evidence also notes that ACE2 glycosylation inhibition studies suggest that sialic acids on ACE2 prevent ACE2–spike interaction, which complicates the interpretation of sialic acid as a co-receptor [N5-F2]. In addition, the evidence is mixed: while some studies suggest sialic acid binding, others indicate that sialic acid may inhibit spike receptor binding [N5-F2]. For HE-containing coronaviruses such as HKU1 and OC43, the evidence supports a role for HE in attachment and receptor destruction, which reduces the need for HE-independent attachment mechanisms in those strains [N3-F3][N2-R4].

Overall, the evidence supports the existence of HE-independent sialic acid interactions and alternative attachment pathways, especially in SARS-CoV-2. However, the support for direct HE-independent sialic acid recognition is weak and mostly speculative. Alternative receptors such as TMPRSS2 and gangliosides can mediate attachment, and host sialic acid can influence spike activation and entry efficiency. The main limitation is that much of the evidence comes from indirect or correlative studies, and the exact molecular mechanisms remain unresolved [N5-F2][N3-F3].
node_outputs.N10:
Limits and controversies in the current evidence base

The current evidence base is mixed in terms of which claims are well-supported versus speculative. The most well-supported claims are that HE is a receptor-destroying enzyme that binds O-acetylated sialic acids and that it is functionally intertwined with the spike protein in coronaviruses [N2-R1][N2-R3][N2-F1]. The evidence also supports that HKU1 uses sialoglycoconjugates and TMPRSS2 as receptors, and that sialoglycan binding can induce conformational changes in the spike protein [N3-F3]. For SARS-CoV-2, the evidence is more suggestive than definitive: the literature reports proposed sialic acid-binding domains, increased binding after neuraminidase treatment, and ganglioside ligands for the spike, but these findings are not universally accepted and have been challenged by studies showing that ACE2 glycosylation can prevent ACE2–spike interaction [N5-F2]. This means that the claim that sialic acid is a major attachment mechanism for SARS-CoV-2 remains controversial and is not yet fully established.

Experimental methods differ substantially across studies. Structural studies use crystallography and mutagenesis to define HE and spike protein interactions [N2-F1]. Functional studies use binding assays, neuraminidase treatment, ACE2 glycosylation inhibition, and pseudotyped virus entry assays to assess attachment and entry efficiency [N5-F2][N3-F3]. Glycan microarray and multivalent display systems are also used to probe receptor specificity [N3-F3]. These methods are powerful but not interchangeable: structural evidence can define molecular contacts, while functional evidence can show whether a protein or sugar is necessary for entry, but both can be confounded by off-target effects or incomplete experimental systems [N2-F1][N5-F2]. The evidence also shows that some findings are derived from in silico predictions, molecular modeling, and microscopy, which are valuable but less direct than biochemical and virological assays [N5-F2].

Major unresolved questions about HE and S cooperation include the precise molecular mechanism of HE’s sialic acid binding site, the extent to which HE directly activates or primes the spike protein, and the exact functional roles of HE in different coronavirus strains [N2-F1][N3-F3]. There is also uncertainty about whether HE is necessary for attachment in all HE-containing coronaviruses. For example, the evidence states that HE may serve primarily as an RDE, but esterase-deficient HE can promote viral spread in vivo, suggesting that HE’s role is not simply to destroy receptors but may also have pleiotropic effects [N2-F1]. Another unresolved issue is whether HE-independent sialic acid interactions are common across coronaviruses or are mostly restricted to SARS-CoV-2 and other atypical cases [N5-F2].

Conflicts between structural, functional, and evolutionary evidence are apparent. In HKU1, the sialoglycan-binding activity and HE are central to attachment and entry, and the study notes that overexpression of ST8SIA1, which produces 9-O-acetylated GD3, promotes HKU1 entry [N3-F3]. This supports the idea that HE/S differences can alter which cell types a virus can infect. For SARS-CoV-2, the evidence suggests that sialic acids may influence entry efficiency and that ACE2 glycosylation can prevent ACE2–spike interaction [N5-F2]. Although SARS-CoV-2 does not use HE as a main attachment protein, the broader coronavirus evidence shows that HE/S differences can shift a virus toward sialic acid-dependent or sialic acid-independent attachment strategies [N5-F2][N3-F3].

## 3) Evidence for HE-independent sialic acid interactions and alternative attachment pathways

### Examples of HE-independent sialic acid recognition or binding
The evidence suggests that HE-independent sialic acid interactions exist, but the support for direct HE-independent sialic acid recognition is thinner than for HE-mediated sialic acid recognition. For SARS-CoV-2, the evidence is speculative and indirect: recent studies have proposed that sialic acids on the host cell surface could serve as co-receptors or attachment factors, and in vitro and ex vivo studies suggest that neuraminidase treatment of cells increases SARS-CoV-2 binding [N5-F2]. Another study proposes a flat sialic acid-binding domain at the N-terminal domain of the spike protein, which may mediate initial contact before higher-affinity ACE2 binding [N5-F2]. However, the evidence also reports that ACE2 glycosylation inhibition studies indicate that sialic acids on ACE2 prevent ACE2–spike interaction, and that gangliosides may serve as ligands for the spike receptor-binding domain [N5-F2]. These findings indicate that sialic acid-related interactions can influence spike activation and entry efficiency, but they do not prove that HE is absent or that sialic acid is the primary attachment mechanism in SARS-CoV-2 [N5-F2].

### Whether alternative receptors or co-receptors mediate sialic acid-like attachment
The evidence explicitly states that HKU1 uses both sialoglycoconjugates and the protein receptor TMPRSS2, and that the D2 domain binds TMPRSS2 only in the up conformation [N3-F3]. This implies that sialic acid binding is not the sole attachment mechanism and that protein receptors can act as co-receptors. In OC43, HE is described as a receptor-destroying enzyme, and the evidence suggests that sialoglycoconjugates are part of the attachment strategy [N2-R4]. In HKU1, the study further notes that ST8SIA1 overexpression promotes entry, indicating that gangliosides downstream of GD3 may be natural receptors [N3-F3]. These examples show that alternative receptors, co-receptors, and carbohydrate receptors can all contribute to attachment and entry.

### How host sialic acid affects spike activation or entry efficiency
Host sialic acid can affect spike activation or entry efficiency in several ways. For HKU1, sialoglycan binding promotes the up conformation of the D2 domain, which is required for protein receptor binding and entry [N3-F3]. In SARS-CoV-2, host sialic acids appear to influence ACE2–spike interaction, with neuraminidase treatment increasing binding and ACE2 glycosylation inhibiting it [N5-F2]. The evidence also suggests that sialic acid can promote spike activation by influencing conformational changes, though the exact mechanism is not fully resolved [N5-F2]. This indicates that host sialic acid is not just a passive bystander but can actively modulate the spike protein’s behavior.

### Limitations of current evidence for HE-independent pathways
The limitations are substantial. The strongest HE-independent evidence comes from SARS-CoV-2, but much of it is indirect or speculative. The literature reports in silico modeling, molecular modeling predictions, microscopy studies, and in vitro/ex vivo data, but these do not establish a direct HE-independent receptor mechanism [N5-F2]. The evidence also notes that ACE2 glycosylation inhibition studies suggest that sialic acids on ACE2 prevent ACE2–spike interaction, which complicates the interpretation of sialic acid as a co-receptor [N5-F2]. In addition, the evidence is mixed: while some studies suggest sialic acid binding, others indicate that sialic acid may inhibit spike receptor binding [N5-F2]. For HE-containing coronaviruses such as HKU1 and OC43, the evidence supports a role for HE in attachment and receptor destruction, which reduces the need for HE-independent attachment mechanisms in those strains [N3-F3][N2-R4].

## 4) Limits and controversies in the current evidence base

### Which claims are well-supported versus speculative
The most well-supported claims are that HE is a receptor-destroying enzyme that binds O-acetylated sialic acids and that it is functionally intertwined with the spike protein in coronaviruses [N2-R1][N2-R3][N2-F1]. The evidence also supports that HKU1 uses sialoglycoconjugates and TMPRSS2 as receptors, and that sialoglycan binding can induce conformational changes in the spike protein [N3-F3]. For SARS-CoV-2, the evidence is more suggestive than definitive: the literature reports proposed sialic acid-binding domains, increased binding after neuraminidase treatment, and ganglioside ligands for the spike, but these findings are not universally accepted and have been challenged by studies showing that ACE2 glycosylation can prevent ACE2–spike interaction [N5-F2]. This means that the claim that sialic acid is a major attachment mechanism for SARS-CoV-2 remains controversial and is not yet fully established.

### How experimental methods differ across studies
Structural studies use crystallography and mutagenesis to define HE and spike protein interactions [N2-F1]. Functional studies use binding assays, neuraminidase treatment, ACE2 glycosylation inhibition, and pseudotyped virus entry assays to assess attachment and entry efficiency [N5-F2][N3-F3]. Glycan microarray and multivalent display systems are also used to probe receptor specificity [N3-F3]. These methods are powerful but not interchangeable: structural evidence can define molecular contacts, while functional evidence can show whether a protein or sugar is necessary for entry, but both can be confounded by off-target effects or incomplete experimental systems [N2-F1][N5-F2]. The evidence also shows that some findings are derived from in silico predictions, molecular modeling, and microscopy, which are valuable but less direct than biochemical and virological assays [N5-F2].

### Major unresolved questions about HE and S cooperation
The main unresolved questions include the precise molecular mechanism of HE’s sialic acid binding site, the extent to which HE directly activates or primes the spike protein, and the exact functional roles of HE in different coronavirus strains [N2-F1][N3-F3]. There is also uncertainty about whether HE is necessary for attachment in all HE-containing coronaviruses. For example, the evidence states that HE may serve primarily as an RDE, but esterase-deficient HE can promote viral spread in vivo, suggesting that HE’s role is not simply to destroy receptors but may also have pleiotropic effects [N2-F1]. Another unresolved issue is whether HE-independent sialic acid interactions are common across coronaviruses or are mostly restricted to SARS-CoV-2 and other atypical cases [N5-F2].

### Conflicts between structural, functional, and evolutionary evidence
Conflicts are apparent. Structural studies of coronavirus HE suggest a distinct receptor-binding site or a separate mechanism from influenza-like HEF, while functional studies indicate that HE and S are functionally intertwined and must balance receptor destruction with receptor binding [N2-F1][N1-R2]. Evolutionary evidence further shows that HE and S coevolve and that functional redundancy exists between HE and S, which complicates interpretation of individual protein roles [N1-R2][N2-F1]. In HKU1, the evidence shows that sialoglycan binding promotes the up conformation of the D2 domain and facilitates protein receptor binding, which conflicts with the simpler view of HE as the sole attachment protein [N3-F3]. In SARS-CoV-2, the evidence is even more conflicted: proposed sialic acid binding is supported by some studies, but others indicate that sialic acids on ACE2 may inhibit spike binding [N5-F2]. These conflicts highlight the need for caution in interpreting HE and S cooperation across coronaviruses.

## 5) Bottom line: cooperation and variation in S/HE function

The overall picture is that S and HE cooperate in a coordinated but not fully redundant way. HE provides reversible sialic acid recognition and receptor destruction, while the spike provides the main receptor-binding activity and fusion function [N2-R1][N2-F1]. In some strains, HE is central to sialic acid recognition and entry, while in others, the spike may rely more on ACE2 or other protein receptors [N2-F1][N3-F3][N5-F2]. Strain-specific differences in receptor specificity and HE/S function arise because HE and S coevolve, and sequence divergence can broaden or narrow receptor preferences [N1-R2][N2-F1][N3-F3].

The evidence supports both direct HE sialic acid binding and indirect effects on spike entry, but the exact molecular details of HE’s receptor-binding site remain partially unresolved [N2-F1][N3-F3]. For HE-independent pathways, the evidence is strongest for SARS-CoV-2 but mostly indirect or speculative, while for HE-containing coronaviruses, HE remains a well-supported RDE [N5-F2][N3-F3]. Overall, the field is still emerging, and the best-supported conclusion is that HE and S work together in sialic acid interactions, but the exact roles and mechanisms vary across coronavirus strains [N1-R2][N2-F1][N3-F3][N5-F2].
